cards.viewer_question: Why were valuable goods brought to mainland quarantine despite deaths aboard?
cards.promise: Trade, warning signs and quarantine decisions.
cards.title: They Brought the Cargo Ashore. Plague Followed.
cards.visual: An official hesitates over a clearance ledger beside an open silk bale inside the Lazaret. No ship.
cards.film_basis: Accepted transcript: valuable textiles, Beaucaire deadline, trade connections, deaths aboard, mainland Lazaret decision; precise transmission remains uncertain.
cards.description:
The Grand Saint-Antoine carried a fortune in silk and cotton—and a growing list of deaths aboard. When the ship reached Marseille, people and valuable goods were sent to a quarantine station on the mainland. Why was this decision made despite the warnings?

Follow the voyage, the pressure of trade and the quarantine choices that preceded the epidemic. The exact route of transmission remains uncertain, but the sequence of warnings, delays and decisions reveals how much was at stake.

cards.viewer_question: What happened to daily life when Marseille was cut off by epidemic?
cards.promise: Life in a trading city whose hospitals and ordinary services were overwhelmed.
cards.title: Marseille 1720: Life Inside a City Cut Off by Plague
cards.visual: Traveler faces a blocked street, guards and shuttered market. No cargo, ships or prison.
cards.film_basis: Accepted transcript: hospitals filled, attempted flight, restrictions, interrupted trade and burial crisis.
cards.description:
What happens when plague cuts off a great trading city? In Marseille, hospitals filled, markets fell silent and the streets became part of an overwhelming emergency. Some residents tried to escape; others remained amid illness, fear and restrictions.

Enter Marseille during the epidemic of 1720 and follow the crisis from the first suspicious deaths to the collapse of ordinary services. This is the story of a city whose quarantine system failed to keep the danger outside—and the people who struggled through the consequences.

cards.viewer_question: Why was the captain freed after a catastrophic voyage and the destruction of his ship?
cards.promise: The captain’s arrest, nearly three years in custody and the case dismissed in 1723.
cards.title: His Ship Burned. Why Was the Captain Set Free?
cards.visual: Close-up of a merchant captain behind prison bars in a stone island cell. No ship, goods or street.
cards.film_basis: Accepted transcript: ship burned near Jarre; Chataud imprisoned at Château d’If; released by court order in 1723. No assertion of deliberate infection or sole responsibility.
cards.description:
The ship was burned. Its captain spent nearly three years in custody. Then the case against him was dismissed. Why did the man who brought the Grand Saint-Antoine home walk free?

Trace Jean-Baptiste Chataud’s voyage, the deaths aboard, the decisions at Marseille’s quarantine station and the catastrophe that followed. From imprisonment at the Château d’If to his release in 1723, his fate raises a question that reaches beyond one captain: how should responsibility be understood when warnings pass through an entire system?
